catalog_quote: [Crowther 1852, Introductory Remarks] Of the accents, none are employed, as in English, merely to mark the stress to be laid on a particular syllable. ... The acute (’) and grave (*) accents are simply marks of intonation— ... i. e. of the rise or fall of the voice—often, as in the Chinese language, ... affecting the signification. ... [p.3, ACCENTS] The Yoruba language is very musical: certain marks to distinguish the tones thus become indispensable. Two accents have therefore been used to point out this distinction, i.e. not to imply that a particular stress is to be laid on the accentuated syllable, but to mark a variety of intonation. ... [p.5] The accent is always indicated when it is on the last syllable; ... sweep_summary: Yoruba (in catalog, coded tonal on Crowther 1852 + Hyman 2005/2012, Laniran & Clements 2003). Six title-hits searched. Two read in full from open copies: Nagano-Madsen 1993 (ISCA archive; scanned, scanned) classes Yoruba as a lexical tone language with F0 the correlate and finds only durational (vowel-lengthening) local prominence bound to H/M tones — confirms tonal; Ehineni 2017 (open-access JUL) is OT reduplication templates, three contrastive tones, zero mentions of stress — silent. Hagberg 2006/1993 (read via the archive.org UMI text; SIL PDF and MPG PuRe copy both refused) mentions Yoruba only for its floating-H object clitic and ATR harmony — not about Yoruba stress. Not obtainable: Siertsema 1959 Lingua 'Stress and tone in Yoruba word composition' (Elsevier closed, no OA copy, no abstract; the only item that names stress for Yoruba — HIGH priority to acquire since it could refine the tonal coding); Nagano-Madsen & Bredvad-Jensen 1995 ICPhS (located in the vol. 3 ToC at 3:652 under the corrected title 'Comparing F0 Reset..', but IPA serves no individual 1995 papers; F0-reset intonation study, low priority); Nagano-Madsen 1992 Lund dissertation on mora/duration (no open copy found; low priority). Nothing read contradicts the catalog; nothing supersedes Crowther 1852 as the deciding source. All downloads and the ToC OCRs are ledgered in (stamp).

new_statements.quote: Eskimo represents a lexical quantity language where duration is the phonetic correlate (Mase and Rischel 1971, Nagano-Madsen 1992) whereas Yoruba represents lexical tone language for which F0 is the phonetic correlate. ... It has been shown that the acoustic property of F0 and duration are utilized in a mutually exclusive way to mark local prominence in the two languages. ... Yoruba, on the other hand, shows wide range of freedom in the lengthening of vowels ... lengthening of vowels were bounded to either high or mid tones, indicating strong correlation between tone and duration.
new_statements.citation: Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko. 1993. The grouping function of F0 and duration in two prosodically diverse languages: Eskimo and Yoruba. Proceedings of the ESCA Workshop on Prosody, Lund, pp. 46-49.
new_statements.reading: Instrumental first-hand study: Yoruba's lexical prosody is tone carried by F0; the only 'local prominence' found is phrase-initial vowel lengthening tied to H/M tones, not a word-level stress. This is a statement of prosodic type (tonal, no word stress described), not a stress-placement rule; it confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every Crowther 1852 and Laniran & Clements 2003 fragment is verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places. The tonal classification is secure: three lexical level tones are documented by a held instrumental study (Laniran & Clements 2003) and two held phonology papers, and the typological literature downloaded now (Hyman 2005 p.172 table 14; Hyman 2012 p.47) explicitly lists Yoruba as tone without stress-accent. sources.citation: Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko. 1993. The grouping function of F0 and duration in two prosodically diverse languages: Eskimo and Yoruba. In: Proceedings of the ESCA Workshop on Prosody, Lund, 27-29 September 1993, pp. 46-49.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Eskimo represents a lexical quantity language where duration is the phonetic correlate (Mase and Rischel 1971, Nagano-Madsen 1992) whereas Yoruba represents lexical tone language for which F0 is the phonetic correlate. ... In Eskimo, where the durational contrast between single and geminated segments dominates the utterances, the local prominence is signalled exclusively by F0 without durational variation. Yoruba, on the other hand, shows wide range of freedom in the lengthening of vowels ... lengthening of vowels were bounded to either high or mid tones, indicating strong correlation between tone and duration.
sources.locator: p. 46 (Introduction); p. 48-49 (Relation between F0 and duration; Conclusion)
sources.note: First-hand instrumental study (text readings and radio news, 3 speakers per language). Yoruba is classed as a lexical tone language with F0 as the lexical correlate; 'local prominence' in Yoruba is durational (vowel lengthening at the start of major constituents, bound to H/M tones), not pitch- or stress-based. Contains no statement of word-stress placement; the only 'lexical stress' mentioned is Germanic. Consistent with the catalog's 'tonal' coding.

sources.citation: Ehineni, Taiwo O. 2017. Prosodic reduplication in Yorùbá. Journal of Universal Language 18(2): 39-59. doi:10.22425/jul.2017.18.2.39
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Yorùbá is a Benue-Congo language spoken in Nigeria and other parts of West Africa. It has a CV syllable structure and has three constrastive tones: low, mid, high. These tones are used to indicate lexical and semantic contrast in the language. i.e., bi (ask), bí (give birth), bì (throw up).
sources.locator: p. 41, section 2 'A Short Background on Yorùbá and Reduplication'
sources.note: 'Prosodic' here means moraic/foot templates for reduplication (base must be bimoraic), in OT. Zero occurrences of 'stress' or 'accent' in the text. States three contrastive lexical tones; silent on word stress. Does not bear on the catalog's classification beyond confirming lexical tone.
